In two protected areas ringed by settlements in the Atlantic Forest of Brazil, now reduced to about one-third of its original extent, researchers from Oswaldo Cruz Institute and the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro captured 1,714 female mosquitoes across 52 species using light traps. DNA analysis of blood meals revealed that 18 of 24 accurately identified samples contained human blood, with others showing dog, rat, bird, and amphibian blood; one specimen carried a mixed amphibian-human blood meal, illustrating flexible host choice. Forest mosquitoes, vectors of yellow fever, Zika, dengue, chikungunya, and Mayaro, thus raise spillover risk as humans near forests become frontline exposure. Habitat loss from human activity accelerates this risk. The findings underscore that ecosystem balance acts as a shield against future outbreaks.

articleHeadline: Monsoon is here and so are the mosquitoes
articleSummary: Masses of monsoon mosquitoes drive dengue, malaria, and chikungunya risk across India, with Delhi-based National Centre for Vector Borne Diseases Control noting 121,824 dengue cases and 100+ deaths in 2025. Three core genetic strategies—Sterile Insect Techniques (SIT), Wolbachia Bacterial Modification (WBM), and Gene Drives (CRISPR-Cas9)—have been deployed to suppress or replace wild mosquitoes in various countries. The United States has allowed localized GMO releases; Brazil conducted wide SIT and WBM releases in urban dengue hotspots; Africa, Australia, and Southeast Asia have run similar programs. Evolutionary resistance and regulatory/ethical hurdles limit effectiveness, with engineered mosquitoes often having lower fitness requiring massive, ongoing releases. The article argues for reduced breeding and early diagnosis, plus lightweight, practical measures (well-lit, dry spaces, white/light walls, screens, and covered water storage) to curb transmission. A world without mosquitoes would prevent over seven lakh deaths annually but disrupt ecosystems.

articleSummary: Viral encephalitis is a dangerous brain infection; about 70% of cases have a viral etiology. It splits into primary viral encephalitis, where viruses directly invade the CNS, and secondary encephalitis, a complication after measles, mumps, or influenza. Japanese encephalitis virus, Herpes Simplex virus, and Epstein–Barr virus are common culprits; Enterovirus causes cases in children. Japanese encephalitis outbreaks typically occur May–July, mainly in children aged 2–8, transmitted by mosquitoes; Enterovirus encephalitis often affects children under 5 from March–June via the digestive route; HSV encephalitis can occur year‑round in both children and adults. Most viral encephalitis lacks specific antiviral therapy, except HSV encephalitis, which can be treated early with antivirals. Management is largely supportive in neurology/ICU settings, to control brain edema, seizures, fever, and vital functions; vaccination is advised for Japanese encephalitis, and mosquito control and hygiene reduce risk. articleSummary: Dengue fever can affect the heart, especially in older adults and people with diabetes, hypertension, kidney disease or heart disease, according to Dr. Harshad Limaye at Nanavati Max Hospital, Mumbai. While most dengue-related cardiac changes are temporary and improve after the infection resolves, delayed care can complicate matters. Dengue can cause myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle) and pericarditis (inflammation around the heart), and may lead to reduced blood flow, low blood pressure, or electrolyte disturbances. Common accompanying changes include bradycardia (unusually slow heart rate). Symptoms such as fatigue, dizziness, fainting, chest discomfort, heart palpitations, or breathlessness should not be ignored, as dengue symptoms can mask heart involvement and may resemble heart attack. Emergency evaluation may include pulse, blood pressure, hydration status, platelet counts, ECG, cardiac enzyme tests, or echocardiography. Do not self-medicate; NSAIDs increase bleeding risk. Paracetamol is a safe option for fever/pain; adequate fluids and rest are important.

Declared May 15, 2026 in Ituri, by July 7, 2026 there were 1,759 laboratory-confirmed cases and 600 deaths (case fatality rate 34.1%). The outbreak moved from Ituri to North Kivu, Kisangani (Tshopo) with two confirmed cases, and reached Haut-Uele, prompting a preventive alert in Kinshasa. The pace—surpassing 80 deaths by mid-May and rising quickly in early July—distinguishes it from prior epidemics. Unlike Zaïre strains, Bundibugyo lacks a vaccine. The Kisangani cases illustrate cross-regional spread along river corridors. In comparison, the 2018–2020 Kivu outbreak caused about 2,280 deaths from ~3,500 cases. UNDP warns up to 10,000 cases and 2,000 deaths by year-end; response hampered by a $20 million funding shortfall and provider strikes in Ituri. Speed of response remains the key variable.
notes: イトゥリ州で宣言後、北キブ、キサンガニ(チョポ州)、ハウトウエレ州に拡大し、キンシャサでも予防警戒。資金不足($2000万)と医療従事者ストライキが対応を阻害。UNDPは年末までに最大1万症例、2000死亡と警告。

articleHeadline: The hunt for hidden TB: How AI is changing India's fight against tuberculosis
articleSummary: VMTB and CATB, two AI tools from Wadhwani AI, advance India's TB control. VMTB uses AI-driven geospatial analytics to predict high-TB-risk areas, integrating TB data with over 20 indicators (population density, air quality, proximity to facilities) on a 500×500-metre grid to generate localized vulnerability rankings for villages and urban wards, guiding targeted active case finding and micro-planning. Integrated with the Ni-kshay portal, Haryana and Assam show improved TB detection. CATB, an offline Android app, analyzes cough sounds and symptoms to screen for presumptive pulmonary TB; after consent and registration, three coughs are recorded and analyzed, with presumptive cases referred for confirmatory tests and Ni-kshay updates. Deployed in 17 states and 148 districts, CATB has screened over 175,000 people aged 7–100, with 12–16% of detected TB cases being asymptomatic. As of 13 July 2026, the approach emphasizes proactive identification to curb transmission.
notes: 結核は既知の流行病であり、本記事はAI技術を用いたスクリーニング・検出手法の紹介記事。新規アウトブレイクや異常事態の報告ではない。

articleSummary: Scrub typhus (Orientia tsutsugamushi) caused a near-fatal multi-organ failure in a 70-year-old woman in Xiamen, Fujian Province, China. After a chigger bite during outdoor work, she developed a sustained fever up to 41°C and rapidly progressed to respiratory, circulatory, renal, hepatic, and coagulation failure, requiring ICU care at Xiamen University Affiliated Haicang Hospital for about two weeks before recovery and discharge. Chiggers inhabit grasses, shrubs, and forested areas; bites are painless due to anesthetic saliva, often leading to delayed diagnosis. The report urges that after outdoor activity, persistent high fever with a painless eschar, along with body aches, fatigue, or rash, warrants prompt medical attention and disclosure of outdoor exposure. Early diagnosis and treatment can reduce fever within 1–3 days and achieve a high cure rate.

articleSummary: China reports 79,000 new COVID-19 cases in June 2026, with 130 severe cases and 1 death from underlying conditions. articleSummary: Dengue risk in Sri Lanka's Western Province is extremely high over the next two weeks as mosquito larvae density rises, with 66,064 dengue cases and 46 deaths recorded this year.
